# Neon Pairs
Neon Pairs is a browser memory game that asks you to find every pair of matching cards.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Reveal two cards at a time and finish in as few moves as you can. A board code repeats a deal, so you can report a problem with the same starting cards.

## Play

Choose a size, then reveal a card and find its partner. Matches stay face up. A miss closes both cards after 800 active milliseconds. Finding every pair completes the game with your moves and time. New Game gives you another deal. Restart repeats the current deal. Full details are in [Rules](gameplay/rules.md).

## Controls

Use mouse, touch or keyboard for the same card action. Keyboard movement, focus, card names and the screen reader journey are in [Input](interface/input.md). The labels and behavior of game and reproduction actions are in [Controls](interface/controls.md).

## Appearance

The game draws faces on a dark background. Shape, marker and fill distinguish each face without color. Layout, colors, motion, 16x16 behavior and zoom are in [Visuals](visuals/visuals.md). The game stays silent as defined in [Sound](sound/sound.md).

## Repeat a game

A board code describes a deal. A snapshot saves progress. A replay records timed actions. The algorithms and version 1 formats are in [Reproducibility](sharing/reproducibility.md). Spec version 2.2 doesn't change those format versions.

## Build

Use React, TypeScript and native DOM controls. Package pins, commands and the offline HTML distribution are in [Technology](architecture/technology.md). Pure game functions, browser effects and behavior placement are in [Architecture](architecture/architecture.md).

Use the journeys in [Acceptance](quality/acceptance.md) to check the finished game. Those examples add no rules beyond the requirement IDs in their defining documents.

## Out of scope

The game doesn't need to support these, so they're never tested:

- Keys and modifier combinations beyond the ones in [Input](interface/input.md#keyboard-movement), which stay with the browser
- Holding a key down
- Several tabs or windows of the game open at once, where each tab may simply overwrite the saved preferences
- How a pointer press behaves when it drifts or is dragged off a card
- Replay or snapshot files with encodings beyond the stated rules, such as a byte-order mark
- Spoken screen-reader output, which stays part of user acceptance as [Input](interface/input.md#screen-reader) describes
- Confirming that a touch long press on a real device opens the context menu without revealing a card, which stays part of user acceptance like spoken output because automated browsers can't produce that gesture

# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.
# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.
# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. [Source layout](source-layout.md) is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, [Architecture](architecture.md) remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.
# Randomness policy

This page explains the boundary between choosing a fresh deal and reproducing a deal in Neon Pairs.

A new board needs an unpredictable seed. A board code, restart, imported snapshot and replay need the opposite property: a particular code always reconstructs the same deck. The implementation keeps those two tasks separate rather than letting a shuffle consult ambient state. [Deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md) covers the deal algorithm as a format; this page concentrates on its source ownership and integration.

## One boundary for fresh input

`src/game/session/fresh-board.ts` exports `freshBoardCode(size, previousSeed?)`. It obtains a seed and returns the normal board-code representation through `boardCode` from `deck.ts`. Only src/game/session/fresh-board.ts may call a random source. Everything else that needs randomness imports it from there. The session controller uses that exported operation when initializing a session or asking for a new game.

The distinction is visible in the imports. `use-game.ts` imports `freshBoardCode` for fresh deals and `createGame` for constructing a game from a code. `game.ts` imports `generateBoard`, which works from supplied data. Nothing in a card component needs to choose a seed, and no deck is shuffled merely because React rendered it.

## Two finite ranges

The fresh-board module uses a one-element `Uint32Array` and `crypto.getRandomValues`. Its possible raw values span the unsigned 32-bit range, with `UINT32_RANGE` set to `2 ** 32`. The allowed seed range is defined in `deck.ts` by `SEED_MAX = 2_147_483_646`. Valid codes use positive seeds, so the transformation adds one after taking a remainder.

The module computes `RANDOM_LIMIT = Math.floor(UINT32_RANGE / SEED_MAX) * SEED_MAX`. With the current values the limit is `4_294_967_292`. A draw below that limit is accepted; one at or above it is retried. Thus each allowed remainder has the same number of accepted raw values. The last four unsigned values do not enter the modulo mapping.

The seed is `(draw % SEED_MAX) + 1`. Its endpoints are therefore 1 and `SEED_MAX`; zero is not produced. The code also checks that `buffer[0]` is defined, which matches the project's checked-index TypeScript setting even though the buffer length is deliberately one. It loops until it can return a valid code.

This is rejection sampling, not rounding a floating-point draw. Applying a plain remainder to all `2 ** 32` possible values would assign a few seeds one more source value than the others. The difference is small numerically, but a reproducible format benefits from an implementation whose range treatment can be described exactly.

## Excluding the immediately previous seed

When `previousSeed` is supplied, a candidate equal to it is discarded. `use-game.ts` passes the current game's seed when creating a new game, including when a different grid size is selected. This means the next seed differs from the immediately preceding seed even across a size change.

That check is narrower than a history of every generated deal. The implementation does not keep a seed registry, does not persist a sequence of fresh codes and does not exclude every seed seen earlier in the session. A code can reappear after intervening games. Nor does the initial call pass an earlier browser session's seed; preferences retain size and best moves, not the last active deal.

The retry loop also does not claim a bounded number of calls. It retries out-of-range draws and an excluded candidate. There is no time-based fallback in this module. A browser crypto failure is not caught here. The storage module's tolerant behavior should not be mistaken for a universal fallback around every browser API.

## Construction after selection

Once the seed is selected, `boardCode(size, seed)` validates the representation. Its format is `np1-SIZE-SEED`, with the supported sizes supplied by `GRID_SIZES`. The parser accepts exactly the seven sizes 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. It also checks that the seed is a safe integer within the allowed maximum.

`createGame(code)` calls `generateBoard(code)` and adds the initial progress fields. The starting deck is already determined by that point. The game starts with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed milliseconds and `started: false`.

The code-producing function can throw for an invalid size or seed. The session's `newGame` action checks the requested size with `isValidSize` before requesting a fresh code. Its normal UI callers use the native select populated from `GRID_SIZES`. These checks protect the application path without adding a second size list to the form.

## Deterministic state is not ambient entropy

`deck.ts` exports `nextRandomState(state)`, but this function is arithmetic over an explicit argument. It computes `(state * 16_807) % 2_147_483_647`. Repeating a call with the same state returns the same result. The name describes a pseudorandom sequence; it does not imply a browser read.

For a valid seed, the generator advances that sequence inside a descending Fisher–Yates shuffle. The initial deck contains two copies of every integer face from zero to `size ** 2 / 2 - 1`, arranged as adjacent duplicates before shuffling. For a 4 by 4 board, it starts as `0, 0, 1, 1` and so on through face 7.

At shuffle position `index`, the number of choices is `index + 1`. The implementation computes a divisible acceptance limit from `SEED_MAX`, advances its local generator state, subtracts one to form the draw, rejects values outside the limit and uses the accepted remainder as the swap position. Both the raw seed selection and the shuffle use rejection, but they operate on different ranges and have different owners.

The maximum multiplication in the sequence is below JavaScript's safe integer limit. The independent browser-test oracle uses BigInt arithmetic, providing a separate expression of the same documented deal rather than calling the production generator to predict itself. [Purity guide](purity-guide.md) explains why explicit state makes these checks possible.

## A concrete stable example

The fixture code `np1-4-1` produces this row-major deck:

```text
6 7 0 5
2 2 0 5
3 7 1 6
4 4 1 3
```

Positions are zero based in rules and formats. Positions 2 and 6 are a pair; positions 0 and 11 are another. The fixture's `EXAMPLE_DECK` stores the whole literal sequence, while `EXAMPLE_PAIRS` lists the matching positions. Those are test facts, not attributes added to hidden cards in the shipped DOM.

Changing the shuffle traversal, recurrence, rejection condition or starting deck would change this example and potentially every shared code. Such a change is therefore observable through board codes, snapshots and replays, even if the interface still looks like a memory game. The generator's determinism connects implementation detail to a public format.

## Every action that chooses or reuses a deal

| Path | Seed behavior in the current implementation |
| --- | --- |
| Initial `useGame` state | Fresh seed using the saved valid size or default size |
| New Game | Fresh seed excluding the current seed |
| Grid-size selection | Fresh seed for the selected size, excluding the current seed |
| Restart | Existing board code passed to `createGame` |
| Load board | Submitted code trimmed, parsed and reconstructed |
| Load snapshot | Decoder validates its code and reconstructs its deck |
| Replay | Reader validates the supplied code and starts from it |

This table is useful when a bug report says that “a new board changed.” A new game is expected to change the seed. A restart or imported code is expected to repeat the existing deal. A size selection is a fresh deal rather than a geometric rearrangement of the old cards.

`newGame` also resets the clock and replaces the session game. Seed choice alone does not clear progress or focus; session replacement and the generation key supply those lifetimes. [Session module](session-module.md) covers that process.

## Evidence and blind spots

`deck.test.ts` covers board-code parsing, generated structure and known vectors. `deck-rejection.test.ts` reads independent BigInt vectors for an over-limit draw and a draw exactly on the shuffle limit. The equality boundary matters because accepting it would break the uniform mapping and alter the deterministic result for that seed.

The browser suite loads documented codes through actual controls and uses `specDeal` from `tests/deal-oracle.ts` when it needs an independent deal. `lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` checks that New Game changes the current code and that a size change chooses a different seed from the previous deal. A complete all-size journey checks that the resulting decks remain playable.

The fresh-board module has no adjacent unit test. Deterministic deck tests establish format behavior and known sequences, rather than statistical properties of the browser entropy source. The raw seed boundary is short enough to inspect directly, but inspection is a different kind of evidence.

The source audit's core list rejects browser entropy references in the named core files. It does not implement a whole-program information-flow proof or a general scanner for every possible source of variation. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes precisely what it scans.

## Diagnosing an unexpected deck

The most useful reproduction is the board code, not the time the game started. Parsing that code reveals both size and seed. Calling `generateBoard` with it establishes the expected deck without involving React or browser state. An imported snapshot reconstructs that same deck and then validates progress against it.

If the code differs, investigate which action replaced the session. If the code agrees but the deck differs, compare the shuffle against the literal vector and independent oracle. If the deck agrees but the wrong art appears, investigate `faceDesign`, reveal state and card props. These are distinct failures with different evidence.

A hidden card deliberately receives `null` as its face prop. Looking for all face identities in its DOM is not a valid debugging strategy for this application boundary. Tests already have the code and can derive a deck independently. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) describes that presentation decision in context.
# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows those cases in detail, and [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runners.

# Test policy

This page explains the verification layers used by Neon Pairs and the kinds of failures each layer can establish.

The repository checks rule transitions, serialized input, source conventions and complete browser journeys. These checks share documented examples but do not all run in the same environment. `npm test` runs Vitest; `npm run test:e2e` builds the current application and diagnostic entries, then uses Node's test runner with Playwright browser support.

## Focused evidence stays near behavior

The core has adjacent tests such as `game.test.ts`, `deck.test.ts`, `snapshot.test.ts` and `replay.test.ts`. Their names make the behavior under discussion easy to locate before reading the whole suite. A feature's rules.ts has a rules.test.ts beside it. Complete interaction journeys remain at the application test level, where focus, storage, browser lifecycle and delivery can be observed together.

Adjacency is useful because a transition and its evidence can be read in one pass. It does not mean every production file in the repository has a one-to-one test file. Some concerns have several focused files: completion, move limits, snapshot selection and replay ordering each get separate attention. Other helpers are exercised through a broader behavior or browser journey.

The architecture specification A10 asks for focused tests near behavior, independent literal generation vectors, transitions checked against stated rules and built HTML checked from disk as well as served. Those are different obligations because no single test environment can establish all of them.

## What Vitest includes

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. It does not include the browser files in `tests`, which end in `.e2e.test.ts` and run under the separate command. There is no hidden browser suite behind `npm test`.

Most unit tests use `node:assert/strict` with `test` imported from Vitest. They call pure functions directly. Clock arithmetic receives numerical observations; session transitions receive a session object; preference tests pass a memory or failing store. This makes failures specific: a mismatch boundary can be checked without waiting for a real timeout.

The script tests also run here. `replay.test.ts` launches child processes to exercise command output and failure exits, and the source-audit files read authored files and configuration. The CLI test has a 60-second timeout because child processes can be slow on a busy verifier. That allowance is test scheduling, not a game timing constant.

## Independence for generated data

A generator test that computes its expected deck using the same generator can prove little about compatibility. The repository instead contains a literal example deck for `np1-4-1`, initial recurrence values and independent rejection vectors. Browser support also has `specDeal` in `tests/deal-oracle.ts`, which expresses the shuffle with BigInt arithmetic.

The rejection tests cover both a draw above the accepted limit and a draw exactly at it. That equality case matters because a one-character comparison change would alter the seeded result. Completion tests iterate supported grid sizes and activate every actual pair to prove that each generated board can finish with one move per pair.

The literal fixture and oracle serve different purposes. A literal fixes a public example. An independent implementation can check more combinations but can still share a mistaken interpretation of the written rule. The documented format, literal vectors and independent arithmetic together provide stronger evidence than any one of them alone.

## State transitions and identity

`activateCard` returns the same state object for ignored input: an invalid index, a matched position, the already revealed first card or input during a mismatch. Tests can check both the unchanged values and reference identity. Identity matters because the session controller and memoized presentation use it to avoid unnecessary work.

A successful first activation changes `started` and selection without adding a move. A second distinct activation adds one move and either matches immediately or opens a mismatch. The rule tests can check this without going through pointer events. Browser journeys then establish that actual buttons call that same path.

The cap tests cover continued matching and victory at `MOVES_MAX = 999_999`, and elapsed-time tests cover the total cap. A limit on the number displayed or serialized is not evidence that play should terminate there. The meaningful regression is whether ordinary transitions still work at the boundary.

## Format validation evidence

Snapshot tests check outer keys, numeric bounds, matched-position consistency and each selection form. `snapshot-selection.test.ts` focuses on nested selection invariants. A selected index must name an available position, a mismatch must involve different faces and complete matched pairs must be represented together. The decoder reconstructs its deck from the code before checking these relationships.

Replay tests add ordering and action count constraints. Equal timestamps preserve array order, while logical time advances before each activation. `replay-order.test.ts` checks a same-time third activation blocked by the preceding mismatch. These are rules about accepted actions, not browser task order.

Round trips establish that the serializer and decoder agree on valid states, but rejection cases are necessary because both could otherwise agree on an overly permissive format. The repository's exact-key helpers and validators make those cases inspectable. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) provide the product-facing definitions.

## Browser command and fresh output

The end-to-end script is:

```sh
npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 "tests/*.e2e.test.ts"
```

The production build type checks first. Both build stages precede the test runner with `&&`, so a failure prevents the suite from opening an older output. `build:art` creates the face sheet and the session harness separately from `dist/index.html`.

The browser wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts` creates a new context per journey and registers its closure with the Node test context. It collects page errors and asserts that none occurred after a successful journey body. It creates an artifact directory from the test name and restricts output paths to a filename. A shared browser and local server are closed in the file-level teardown.

The standard journey timeout is 30 seconds and the long one is 90 seconds. Playwright assertions use a 15-second configured timeout. These values make verification tolerant of busy machines; they do not lengthen the logical mismatch interval, which controlled-clock tests exercise precisely.

## Disk and HTTP evidence

`tests/game-fixture.ts` defines a `file:` URL for the distribution and separate URLs for the two diagnostic builds. `tests/artifact-server.ts` also serves the built HTML on an ephemeral loopback port, accepting only `/`. This is a test server around the finished file, not the Vite development server.

Disk delivery demonstrates that the HTML carries its own code and assets. HTTP-origin journeys establish preference persistence in a browser environment with a stable storage origin for the journey. A result from one mode does not establish the other, because storage behavior on local files varies.

`build-output.e2e.test.ts` reads the HTML and checks for the excluded fetch and module-preload markers. Browser journeys can additionally watch requests. Source inspection, artifact inspection and actual browser behavior contribute different evidence about offline delivery. [Offline delivery](offline-delivery.md) explains why all three are useful.

## Browser interactions that pure tests cannot see

Arrow navigation tests can check the helper's target arithmetic directly, but only the browser can show where focus lands, whether Tab leaves and whether scrolling keeps the focus ring visible. Native click behavior also matters for keyboard activation, context menus and touch scrolling. The card component uses the native click path rather than a separate game action per input method.

Artwork tests render all 128 faces through the real `Card` component in the separate face sheet. Layout journeys cover large boards, visible scrollbars, zoom and touch. Accessibility journeys inspect the Chromium accessibility tree through a complete keyboard interaction. The README explicitly separates this tree evidence from a spoken screen-reader acceptance journey.

These distinctions prevent overclaiming. A passing tree check does not mean a human has listened to every announcement. A passing layout measurement does not mean every browser family has been tested. [Browser support](../quality/browser-support.md) and [Accessibility audit](../quality/accessibility-audit.md) are the related places for that evidence.

## Time and lifecycle regressions

The clock tests are intentionally layered. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks arithmetic, while `session.test.ts` checks stale generations and paused state. Browser files exercise hidden intervals, idle pause periods, fractional observations and exports between timer callbacks.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` overrides the observed clock and sends an overdue click in the same browser task. No scheduled timer can run first, so this isolates the controller's synchronize-before-activate behavior. `idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` avoids inspecting the game repeatedly during inactivity, exposing bugs that an incidental export synchronization could otherwise mask.

The session harness makes teardown observable by unmounting the actual game. `timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timers and visibility listeners, checks that one active timer exists, then checks cleanup after unmount. It also follows an earlier mismatch with a later mismatch in the same deal. This catches mistakes that merely changing the deal generation would not expose.

## Source and runtime records

[Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) records the package, compiler, source and naming patterns inspected by the static checks. Browser setup separately writes its observed runtime versions and can enforce the named combination. These records describe different evidence; neither replaces a behavior test.

For a review, the useful account names the changed behavior and the check that observes it. [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) gives examples of that mapping.

# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in [competition deals](competition-deals.md).

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterfinal | 4 | 16 | 8 |
| Semifinal | 6 | 36 | 18 |
| Final | 8 | 64 | 32 |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md). The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

[Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md), [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) and [card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [layout grid](../visuals/layout-grid.md) and [zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md).

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md) covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md) explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.

[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
# Shared-device competition

This page explains the purpose, scope and implementation context of shared-device competition in Neon Pairs.

Competition gives a group gathered around one device a reason to return to the board together. It is intended for the small social setting: a family laptop, a tablet passed around a table, or a few people taking a break at the same desk. The interesting product question is how individual memory play becomes a shared occasion without losing the clarity of the existing game.

## Where the product stands

The game implements solo play. There is no competition entry form, bracket view, participant model or tournament controller in `src/game/Game.tsx`. That component composes the ordinary controls, status, board and reproduction panel around `useGame()`. Competition is a product extension that has not yet shipped.

This distinction matters during review. A prototype can show a convincing bracket around the existing board while still delegating all game actions to the ordinary session. That demonstrates a possible composition, but it says little about whether participant progress, handoffs and completion belong to the same coherent experience. The detailed pages identify the relevant behavior and the places where the current source offers support or creates a complication.

The existing specification is version 2.2. It describes a local browser memory game, its reproducibility tools and its browser session. It does not describe a competition flow. The additional decisions for this scope live in the linked competition pages; this overview introduces their purpose without reproducing them.

## Why share a device

A shared screen makes the activity visible. People can talk about the artwork, remember a near miss and recognize the effort behind another person's finish. There is no remote opponent waiting behind a network connection, and no account setup between the group and the game. The game already has a compact delivery model: the built game can be opened from one HTML file.

Sharing hardware also changes what people expect. On a personal device, a result feels like part of that person's practice. On a shared tablet, the person holding it may have changed several times since the page opened. A familiar status area can therefore carry a different social meaning even when its numbers are technically correct. The distinction between a person's current attempt, the group's progress and the device's ordinary records is especially easy to blur.

Competition is useful when it gives those existing actions a context people can follow. It is less useful when the group spends more attention administering the session than remembering cards. This is why the research discussion concentrates on interruptions, orientation and the physical act of passing the device, rather than treating the bracket drawing as the whole feature.

## Three things people are following

An individual concentrating on a board is following card positions and remembered faces. Someone waiting nearby is following the social event: who is occupied, whether a finish is close and when attention will return to the group. The person explaining the game is following the application itself, often watching for a control that might replace the current position.

These perspectives overlap, but they are not interchangeable. A board full of exposed faces is meaningful to the current player. It gives a waiting person relatively little information about where the group is in its event. A compact event view can answer that social question, while the ordinary board remains the place where the player thinks.

The competition documents separate these subjects so that readers can find the relevant decision without extracting it from a long screen-by-screen walkthrough. [Pairing](competition-pairing.md) covers the relationship between entrants and the bracket. [Rounds](competition-rounds.md) covers event stages. [Boards](competition-boards.md) and [deals](competition-deals.md) distinguish the dimensions of a board from its actual arrangement. [Ties](competition-ties.md) and [scores](competition-scores.md) address results from different angles.

## A local social activity, with local evidence

The current project has no backend or account service. Its board codes and exported progress are useful for reproducing a situation, not for establishing the identity of a person who played it. That is a comfortable fit for a group that is physically present and can see what happened. It is a much weaker basis for claims about distant strangers.

The same limitation applies to development evidence. A replay can help an engineer understand a sequence of card actions. A screenshot can help someone understand what the group saw. Neither explains why a participant handed the tablet back early, or whether someone had been watching another person's screen. Those are observations about the setting, and they belong in the research account rather than in an assertion about the game engine.

[Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) explains the existing technical tools. [Competition research](competition-research.md) describes local sessions and the limits of drawing conclusions from them. The two accounts answer different questions and are useful together.

## How the current code helps

The core already separates game data from presentation. `src/game/game.ts` contains card transitions and logical elapsed time. `src/game/deck.ts` contains board parsing and deterministic generation. Those files have no participant knowledge. That makes them a useful basis for discussing competition without embedding group administration into card rendering.

The browser session is a separate layer under `src/game/session`. It owns the bridge between that core and React, browser visibility, clock observations and preferences. This is the most consequential boundary for an extension: reusing a visual component is easy to notice, while inheriting a session side effect can remain hidden until much later.

The board itself lives under `src/game/board`. Its card buttons and navigation code operate on positions. The status view receives a game and a best value; it does not discover an event or a participant. [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md), [session module](../architecture/session-module.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) give the broader engineering context.

# Competition pairing

This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition.

Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller.

## From the entry list to the opening matches

Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people.

The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match.

Here is a worked example with eight entrants.

| Entry position | Entrant | Seed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First | Ada | 1 |
| Second | Bo | 2 |
| Third | Cora | 3 |
| Fourth | Dev | 4 |
| Fifth | Emi | 5 |
| Sixth | Finn | 6 |
| Seventh | Gia | 7 |
| Eighth | Hal | 8 |

Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved.

## What a seed means here

In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one.

This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above.

There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects.

[Competition deals](competition-deals.md) covers board identity. [Competition ties](competition-ties.md) covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here.

## The small example catches a different mistake

With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list.

That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order.

It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list.

## A pairing review on paper

A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada.

This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction.

The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md), and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in [competition scores](competition-scores.md).

For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately.

## Unresolved pairing decisions

The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two.

These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope.

# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device.
